raw: {"slots": {"question": [{"claim": "Whether the Democratic 'convicted criminal' label on Trump spilled over to Democrats' perceptions of people with criminal records and of representation, and whether a counter-narrative could offset any such spillover.", "quotes": [{"text": "propagating such labels on Trump may thereby spillover, impacting constituents’ perspectives of individuals with records more broadly", "page": 1}]}, {"claim": "Asks whether the Democratic Party's use of stigmatizing rhetoric to win the 2024 election was worth the potential harm to the roughly 77 million people with criminal records.", "quotes": [{"text": "When reflecting on the decision to employ this stigmatizing rhetoric in an effort to secure the 2024 Presidential Election, the Democratic Party made its choice, perhaps at the expense of 77 million individuals with criminal records", "page": 18}]}, {"claim": "Argues against the use of stigmatizing terms: acknowledging Trump's convictions was likely necessary, but using stigmatizing labels to do so was not.", "quotes": [{"text": "Though acknowledgement of Trump's convictions by the Democratic Party was likely unavoidable and in fact, necessary, the use of stigmatizing terms was not.", "page": 2}]}, {"claim": "Challenges the view that Democrats' less punitive justice policy preferences mean they hold positive perceptions of people with records, since policy support is distinct from perceptions of those affected.", "quotes": [{"text": "policy support is distinct from perceptions of individuals who would be directly impacted by these policies.", "page": 3}]}], "central_claim": [{"claim": "Exposure to the Trump ad labeling him a 'convicted criminal' lowered Democrats' perceptions of people with records, and a formerly system-involved representative's perspective shown before the ad largely offset that effect.", "quotes": [{"text": "Findings suggest that the counter-stereotype vastly ameliorated the negative effects of the advertisement on Democrats’ perceptions of individuals with criminal records.", "page": 1}]}], "evidence": [{"claim": "The evidence is a survey experiment with 2,439 self-identified Democrats in the U.S., assigned roughly evenly to a control group, a Trump ad alone group, and a counter-narrative first group. The ad was a Trump mugshot labeled 'CONVICTED CRIMINAL'. The survey was fielded through Prolific.", "quotes": [{"text": "the 2,439 participants were allocated approximately evenly across one of three different treatment groups", "page": 4}, {"text": "President Donald J. Trump’s mugshot, which was labeled, in all capital letters, “CONVICTED CRIMINAL.”", "page": 5}, {"text": "The survey was fielded through Prolific, an online survey platform that is commonly utilized for conducting survey-based research", "page": 8}]}, {"claim": "The counter-narrative is an edited excerpt from a 2024 Nevada Current news article about a formerly incarcerated state lawmaker, with the state and the lawmaker's first name removed.", "quotes": [{"text": "This excerpt was from the article entitled, “Could a formerly incarcerated lawmaker reshape justice policy in the NV Legislature?,” by Michael Lyle, published in the Nevada Current on November 5, 2024 [55].", "page": 5}]}, {"claim": "Perceptions of individuals with criminal records were measured with a five-item index of Likert agreement statements, with reliability that the author describes as acceptable but at the lower end.", "quotes": [{"text": "The perceptions of individuals with criminal records outcome included an index, where participants were presented with five statements and were asked how much they agreed with each on a seven-point Likert scale", "page": 7}]}, {"claim": "Responses were screened for data quality, including attention checks, duplicate and incorrect completion codes, and a reCAPTCHA score to flag likely bots, which removed about 1.69% of the remaining responses.", "quotes": [{"text": "Specifically, these scores range from zero to one, where values above 0.50 are purported to be likely human responses [61].", "page": 8}, {"text": "Approximately 1.69% of responses post-removal of duplicates, incorrect/no codes, and failed attention checks were flagged as not being a likely human response, and were also dropped.", "page": 8}]}, {"claim": "The analysis compares treatment effects between participants who identified as system-impacted and those who did not, a subgroup split of 521 and 1,918 participants.", "quotes": [{"text": "in regard to the heterogeneity of treatment by whether someone identified themselves as being systemimpacted (n = 521) or not (n = 1,918)", "page": 13}]}], "key_findings": [{"claim": "Exposure to the Trump ad alone significantly lowered Democrats' positive perceptions of individuals with criminal records relative to no ad exposure.", "quotes": [{"text": "exposure to the Trump advertisement alone significantly decreased positive perceptions of individuals with criminal records", "page": 11}]}, {"claim": "Placing a system-impacted state representative's perspective before the ad almost entirely offset the ad's negative effect on perceptions of people with records.", "quotes": [{"text": "when paired with (and preceded by) a counter-narrative of a dedicated, system-impacted state representative who speaks to the harm of the “criminal” label, these effects were almost entirely ameliorated", "page": 15}]}, {"claim": "The counter-narrative significantly reduced support for the Trump ad compared with the ad alone.", "quotes": [{"text": "exposure to the counter-narrative significantly decreased support for the Trump advertisement, relative to the Trump advertisement alone", "page": 11}]}, {"claim": "Exposure to the Trump ad alone significantly increased respondents' feelings of being well represented and their belief that officials serve the public, a result the authors did not hypothesize for representation quality.", "quotes": [{"text": "Additionally, exposure to the Trump advertisement significantly increased feelings of being well represented by elected officials", "page": 15}]}, {"claim": "The effects of the ad and counter-narrative on perceptions of people with records were larger for system-impacted respondents than for others.", "quotes": [{"text": "In terms of relative magnitude, the effects were greater for those who identified as being system-impacted, compared to those who did not", "page": 14}]}], "scope_and_limits": [{"claim": "The design was not a full factorial, so the counter-narrative's effect alone cannot be isolated from the Trump ad, since the counter-narrative arm always includes the ad.", "quotes": [{"text": "the counter-narrative arm cannot be directly compared to the pure control arm to test the impact of the counter-narrative alone because it also involves exposure to the Trump advertisement.", "page": 16}]}, {"claim": "The study was conducted in July 2025, after the election, so the results may not hold during a campaign.", "quotes": [{"text": "this current study was conducted in July of 2025, after the outcome of the election was known and not actively during the campaign", "page": 17}]}, {"claim": "The authors describe the study as preliminary and say well-powered field experiments are needed to confirm and extend the findings.", "quotes": [{"text": "While well-powered and aptly-timed field experiments are needed to confirm and extend these findings", "page": 1}]}, {"claim": "The advertisement's image and its stigmatizing text were presented together in every arm, so the study cannot separate the effect of the mugshot from the effect of the 'convicted criminal' wording.", "quotes": [{"text": "as the advertisement (i.e., Trump’s mugshot with the words ‘convicted criminal’ imposed on the image) was presented consistently across treatment arms, it is not possible to disentangle the impact of the image from the stigmatizing terminology imposed", "page": 17}]}], "theoretical_positioning": [{"claim": "The authors place the study within social categorization theory and extend it to argue that a stigmatizing label applied to one salient group member spills over to the wider category of people with records.", "quotes": [{"text": "social categorization theory [12–15] would suggest that the effects of utilizing this label likely spilled over.", "page": 2}]}, {"claim": "The authors offer Prospect Theory as a possible account of the finding that the Trump ad raised ratings of other officials, treating Trump as a reference point.", "quotes": [{"text": "Collectively, these results may simply be Prospect Theory in action: Donald J. Trump may be serving as reference point that may influence Democrats to see other elected officials as comparatively better", "page": 15}]}, {"claim": "The authors position perspective-getting, a framework from political science and psychology, as the messaging approach they propose as an alternative to stigmatizing campaign labels, and they build their counter-narrative on it.", "quotes": [{"text": "Alternatively, one presumably unexplored messaging intervention in the 2024 election – though heavily supported by political science and psychological literature – is perspective-getting", "page": 3}]}, {"claim": "The authors combine affective and policy-based accounts of representation, arguing that a counter-narrative with both a personal perspective and a policy signal addresses both routes to political support.", "quotes": [{"text": "would be well-suited to addressing both the affective and policy representation avenues for bolstering support.", "page": 4}]}, {"claim": "The authors weigh a deservingness account against a stigma-reduction account of their results and favor stigma reduction, based on the empirical link between attitudes and personal connection, while noting the alternative as possible.", "quotes": [{"text": "While it is possible that the intervention constructs a new category of deservingness, rather than reducing stigma, the empirical relationship between attitudes and personal connection suggests that reduction of stigma is more likely", "page": 16}]}], "interlocutor_claim": [{"claim": "Prior literature shows that labels such as 'criminal' cause worse perceptions of people with records than person-first language. The authors take this as the basis for expecting the Trump label to harm perceptions of people with records.", "quotes": [{"text": "Extant literature highlights the causal impact of propagation of labels, such as ‘criminal’, to significantly worsen perceptions of individuals with records, relative to more humanizing, person-first language", "page": 2}]}, {"claim": "A study by Grüning and Schubert found that anger-inducing political ads boosted support and action mainly among members of the party that ran the ad. The authors use this to frame why a Democratic ad might be expected to work.", "quotes": [{"text": "For example, one study found that anger-inducing political advertisements bolstered support and encouraged action specifically amongst members of the party producing the advertisement [33].", "page": 3}]}, {"claim": "Experimental work is cited as showing that policy positions and officials acting on them affect feelings of being represented more strongly than affect does. The authors use this to argue that representation-related outcomes matter alongside emotional appeals.", "quotes": [{"text": "experimental evidence suggests that policy positions and elected officials taking action tend to have a stronger causal effect on feelings of being represented, rather than affect [37].", "page": 3}]}, {"claim": "A meta-analysis is cited as finding no empirical support for negative campaign advertising helping electoral success. The authors use this to question the Democratic Party's use of stigmatizing attacks.", "quotes": [{"text": "meta-analytic evidence does not empirically support the use of negative campaign advertisements to aid election success [7].", "page": 2}]}, {"claim": "Some evidence is cited that incarceration shifts political ideology further to the right. The authors qualify this, saying it is unclear whether the shift would persist outside status-quo political messaging about records.", "quotes": [{"text": "Though some evidence suggests that experiencing incarceration may serve to shift ideologies further to the right [54]", "page": 4}]}, {"claim": "Recent experimental work is cited as suggesting that affective polarization may not meaningfully affect political outcomes, though it may matter for interpersonal dynamics. The authors draw on this when discussing how emotional appeals may work.", "quotes": [{"text": "recent robust experimental work suggests that affective polarization may not have meaningful impact on political outcomes, though may have some implications for interpersonal dynamics", "page": 3}]}]}}
